There is no scientific evidence supporting the claim that 5G technology is linked to the spread or causation of COVID-19. COVID-19 is primarily transmitted through respiratory droplets when an infected person coughs, sneezes, or speaks, and can also spread by touching contaminated surfaces and then touching the face; it is not transmitted via electromagnetic frequencies or wireless networks such as 5G [2, p.2]. Extensive research has shown that the electromagnetic frequencies used in 5G technology are non-ionizing, meaning they do not have the energy required to break chemical bonds, alter cellular structures, or directly influence viral replication [2, p.3]. A 2022 study published in the "Telecommunication and Public Health Journal" confirmed that non-ionizing radiation, such as that from 5G, cannot carry or activate viral particles [2, p.3]. Furthermore, international health and telecommunication authorities, including the International Commission on Non-Ionizing Radiation Protection (ICNIRP), have established safety standards for 5G networks, and these networks are considered safe for public health [2, p.4]. Experts in epidemiology and public health have emphasized that linking 5G to COVID-19 is a distraction from proven preventive measures such as vaccination, mask-wearing, and social distancing [2, p.4]. The consensus among scientists and health authorities is that there is no connection between 5G technology and the causation or facilitation of COVID-19 [2, p.5]. Misinformation about such connections can actually harm public health efforts by diverting attention from effective strategies to control the pandemic [2, p.5].
